unitDescription.value:
In this Year 8 Industrial Technology and Design unit, students design and manufacture a personalised wooden port or suitcase. They develop practical woodworking skills through measuring, marking, cutting, chiselling, joining, sanding and finishing timber, with particular emphasis on accurately producing finger joints and safely using workshop tools and equipment.

Students use the SBC Design Model to investigate existing products, develop ideas and repurpose the standard wooden port for a practical use, such as storing fishing equipment, art supplies, stationery, medals or personal items. They communicate their improved design through annotated sketches and a dimensioned SketchUp model before constructing and evaluating the finished product.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: Students at St Brendan’s College operate within a diverse learning environment where practical, hands-on application is essential to engagement and skill acquisition. The Year 7–8 Design Technologies curriculum is structured to accommodate varying levels of prior experience with digital systems and manual production techniques. Learning experiences leverage the College’s commitment to vocational pathways and technical literacy, ensuring that students develop fundamental design-thinking skills alongside an appreciation for safety, sustainability, and material performance. Tasks are designed to build student confidence through scaffolded inquiry and iterative prototyping, providing frequent opportunities for students to connect design solutions to authentic, real-world community contexts. Literacy and numeracy support is integrated across all units, ensuring students can effectively communicate design proposals and analyse project data. Teachers differentiate instruction to support the specific needs of the cohort, fostering resilience and independent problem-solving through reflective practice and iterative design cycles that align with the achievement standards of the Australian Curriculum.

description.value:
Students complete three connected components:

Safety and theory tasks covering workshop procedures, risk assessment, timber, tools, fasteners, joints and finishing processes.
A design folio documenting the SBC Design Model: defining the problem, researching existing products, brainstorming, sketching, self-evaluating and producing a final dimensioned SketchUp design.
A practical wooden port manufactured to the supplied dimensions and personalised for an identified purpose.

Students are assessed on their understanding of materials, tools and production processes; development and communication of design ideas; safe and accurate workshop practices; management of the production process; quality and functionality of the completed port; and evaluation of their design and finished product.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 8 students explain how people design, innovate and produce products, services and environments for preferred futures. For each of the 4 prescribed technologies contexts they explain how the features of technologies impact on design decisions, and create designed solutions based on analysis of needs or opportunities. Students create and adapt design ideas, processes and solutions, and justify their decisions against developed design criteria that include sustainability. They communicate design ideas and solutions to audiences using technical terms and graphical representation techniques, including using digital tools. They independently and collaboratively document and manage production processes to safely produce designed solutions.

activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Reference:
1. SBC Design Model: A structured, four-phase engineering and design framework (Investigate, Ideate, Produce, Evaluate) used at St Brendan's College.
2. Hierarchy of Control: A systematic six-to-five tier model used to eliminate or minimise workplace hazards, ordered from most effective to least effective.
3. Hazard: Any condition, equipment, substance, or action in the workshop with the potential to cause injury, damage, or illness.
4. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Clothing or wearable devices designed to create a protective barrier between the student and workshop hazards.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Hierarchy of Hazard Control in the Workshop
activities.teacherDoes: Present the five key tiers of hazard control used in school workshops: Elimination, Substitution, Engineering Controls, Administrative Controls, and PPE. activities.scaffolding:
Hierarchy order (most to least effective):
1. Elimination (physically remove hazard)
2. Substitution (replace with safer alternative)
3. Engineering controls (isolate people mechanically from the hazard)
4. Administrative controls (change procedures, training, and signs)
5. PPE (protect the worker with personal gear)

prompt: Why does a chisel split timber easily along the grain but stall when pushed across end grain?

activities.scaffolding:

2. Timber Density: The mass of wood substance per unit of volume (kg/m³), which directly influences the hardness, weight, and strength of the timber.
3. End Grain: The exposed cross-cut surface of a board where the hollow ends of the vertical wood cells are visible perpendicular to the length.

activities.title: Chisel Anatomy, Sharpening & Mallet Technique
activities.teacherDoes:
Gather students around the main demonstration bench behind the yellow perimeter safety line. Demonstrate chisel anatomy (bevel cutting edge, flat back, shank, handle). Model sharpening on oil/water stones: holding the chisel bevel flat at 25–30 degrees, moving in a smooth figure-eight stroke to hone the edge, and lapping the flat back to remove the burr. Explicitly demonstrate securing timber in a bench vice, maintaining both hands behind the cutting edge, and striking the chisel with a wooden mallet, highlighting why steel hammers are strictly forbidden.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'Watch my wrist angle on the sharpening stone—locked at 25 degrees, moving in a figure-eight to distribute wear evenly. Notice how my left hand guides the tip while my right hand controls the push stroke. When striking, I use only a wooden mallet to preserve the impact handle.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration from behind the safety line. Complete the workbook annotation task by recording the name and function for each of the four numbered callouts on the chisel and striking tool diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the demonstration, then complete the 4 numbered callouts on the chisel diagram in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must you never strike a woodworking chisel with a steel claw hammer?
expected: Steel hammers mushroom or shatter wooden and plastic chisel handles, sending sharp fragments flying and destroying the tool.
question: Why must both hands remain behind the cutting edge at all times during paring?
expected: If the chisel slips off the timber workpiece, keeping hands positioned behind the cutting edge prevents catastrophic puncture wounds or lacerations.

Callout Components:
1 = Cutting Edge Bevel (Ground at 25–30 degrees to shear timber fibres cleanly)
2 = Blade & Shank (Solid tool steel transmitting mallet force)
3 = Impact Handle (Ergonomic wooden or composite grip designed for striking)
4 = Wooden Mallet (Broad timber face that cushions impact without mushrooming chisel handles)

activities.title: Supervised Practice: Honing and Paring Stance
activities.teacherDoes: Rotate between sharpening stations in small supervised groups. Guide each student to position the chisel bevel flat on the lubricated oil/water stone at 30 degrees, guide their hands through 10 smooth strokes, and demonstrate checking for a micro-burr on the back. Supervise the initial paring cut on scrap softwood clamped firmly in a vice, actively correcting body stance and two-handed grip. Modelled example: 'Notice how my left hand stays locked on the handle while my right hand guides the neck, keeping my fingers safely behind the steel bolster at all times.'
activities.studentsDo: Perform chisel sharpening strokes on stones and complete test paring cuts under direct teacher supervision, ticking each performance criterion in their workbook checklist upon successful execution.
activities.visibleInstructions: Hone your chisel on the sharpening stone and execute test paring cuts in the vice. Tick off each checklist item as demonstrated.
activities.questioning:
How can you tell if the bevel is sitting completely flat on the sharpening stone? Expected: You feel the bevel 'lock' flat against the stone surface without rocking forward onto the tip or backward onto the heel.
Why is a dull chisel significantly more dangerous to operate than a razor-sharp chisel? Expected: A dull chisel resists cutting, causing the user to apply excessive force which leads to sudden slips and loss of control.
activities.scaffolding:
Execution Sequence:
1. Apply 3 drops of honing oil / water to stone surface.
2. Rest bevel flat on stone (feel the facet lock).
3. Maintain wrist angle and hone in smooth figure-8 motion.
4. Flip chisel flat on back to hone off the wire edge/burr.
5. Clamp timber in vice and pare with two hands on the tool.

workbookSpec.title: Face Side Dressing Procedure Sequence
workbookSpec.prompt: Identify and record the four critical steps for dressing and checking the face side of timber stock.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:

3. Flatness and Twist Check: Place steel rule diagonally across corners to verify absence of twist/wind.
4. Face Mark: Pencil standard cabinetmaker's mark on the true surface pointing towards reference edge.

activities.title: Joint Anatomy: Technical Callouts and Grain Direction
activities.teacherDoes: Project a dimensioned isometric diagram of an interlocking finger joint onto the board. Explicitly define Pin, Socket, Shoulder Line, and Waste Wood using professional QCAA terminology. Demonstrate the cross-hatching convention used in woodworking to designate waste material. activities.questioning:
question: Why do finger joints offer significantly higher tensile strength than standard end-grain butt joints?
expected: Finger joints provide extensive long-grain to long-grain gluing surfaces, which form robust chemical bonds, unlike porous end grain that merely absorbs adhesive without structural bonding.
question: What is the operational function of the scribed shoulder line during marking out?
expected: It defines the exact depth stop for both pins and sockets, ensuring all joint faces sit perfectly flush and square when finally assembled.
activities.scaffolding:
Key definitions:
- Pin: The projecting timber tongue left standing after waste removal.
- Socket: The recess cut out between pins to accept the mating member.
- Shoulder Line: The continuous reference line marked at 90 degrees across all faces at timber thickness depth.
- Waste Wood: Material designated for removal, marked with cross-hatching ('X') to prevent cutting errors.

activities.title: Generative Workshop Practice: Chisel Mechanics and Failure Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Model the mechanics of a chisel blade acting as an inclined wedge. Explain why striking a chisel deeply across the grain splits pine along its longitudinal fibres. Demonstrate the correct 'step-down' technique: removing 2mm to 3mm chips from the end grain working backwards toward the shoulder line. Highlight the two-hands-behind-the-cutting-edge rule.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the analysis section explaining the wedge effect, outline the step-down paring procedure, and write the 3-2-1 workshop safety reflection.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the written responses in your workbook: explain why timber splits under heavy chisel strikes, describe the step-down method, and complete the 3-2-1 reflection.
activities.questioning: What causes timber to split uncontrollably when a chisel is driven straight down the shoulder line on the first blow? Expected: The bevel acts as a wedge, forcing fibres apart along their natural grain boundary ahead of the cutting edge and splitting the timber below the line. Why must the flat face of the bevel-edge chisel face the shoulder line during final paring? Expected: The flat back provides a straight reference plane against the scribed groove, ensuring a vertical 90-degree socket floor.
activities.scaffolding:
Key safety and technique principles:
- Always secure the workpiece in a vice or clamp to a bench hook.
- Both hands must remain behind the chisel cutting edge at all times.
- Step-down method: cut small 2mm terraces toward the shoulder rather than attempting full-depth removal in one strike.
- Work from both timber faces to prevent back-face breakout.

question: Why must the marking knife sever the timber fibres before sawing begins?
expected: Knife cuts cleanly sever tough surface grain, preventing the saw teeth from splintering or tearing the edge fibres as they enter the cut.

expected: Align the forearm, wrist, and saw spine directly in line with the marked line, rocking gently from the shoulder with feet planted in a stable boxer's stance.

activities.teacherDoes: Supervise independent practical cutting at workshop benches. question: Why must you stop sawing the instant your teeth touch the scribed shoulder line?

question: How do you prevent tear-out on the back face of your socket during chiselling?

- Check saw depth on both front and rear edges simultaneously.

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define and model the three core engineering terms: 'Tolerance', 'Radial Movement', and 'Flush Fit'. Use physical timber test joints to demonstrate the difference between a bind, an interference fit, and an acceptable clearance fit. Script: 'In Yeppoon's humid coastal climate, timber continually absorbs ambient moisture. If we fabricate joints with zero tolerance, radial swelling across the grain will split the corners of your box. We design for a precise 0.1 to 0.2 mm clearance.'
activities.studentsDo: Record the definitions for tolerance, radial movement, and flush fit in the workbook table, referencing the teacher's modelled test joints and scaffolding notes.
activities.visibleInstructions: Define the 3 timber engineering terms in your workbook table based on the explicit instruction and provided scaffolding.
activities.questioning:
q: Why will a joint cut with zero tolerance fail during a humid Yeppoon summer?
Expected: The timber fibres absorb moisture from the air, swelling across the grain and generating internal pressure that splits the joint corners.
q: How does a planned tolerance of 0.1 to 0.2 mm prevent joint binding without causing structural wobble?
Expected: It leaves enough room for wood movement and PVA glue film without loosening the interlocking mechanical hold.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions to record:
- Tolerance: The planned, allowable variation or gap between mating components to allow assembly without binding.
- Radial Movement: The expansion and contraction of timber cells across the growth rings due to changes in environmental moisture.
- Flush Fit: A condition where two adjoining timber faces or joint ends align perfectly on the same flat geometric plane.
activities.eLearning: Project cross-section diagrams of seasonal timber cell expansion to illustrate radial versus longitudinal dimensional change.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the vocabulary of timber movement, let us examine how cellular structure governs structural joint design through guided notes.

activities.title: Precision Baseline Scribing Demonstration
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate setting the marking gauge using the actual thickness of the mating timber board rather than a steel rule. Model the proper grip: fence registered firmly against the face side, rolling the gauge forward to let the spur scribe a clean, shallow line across both faces and edges. Emphasise marking waste: immediately shade the waste areas with a clear pencil 'X'. Script: 'If the gauge fence wobbles away from your face edge, your baseline wanders, and your pins will either stand proud or seat recessed. The spur must cut wood fibres cleanly to create a tracking track for the saw.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration, focusing on the gauge angle and fence contact. Complete the workbook diagram annotation identifying the four critical marking components before setting their own gauges.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the 4 callouts on the joint marking diagram in your workbook: Reference Face, Scribed Baseline, Waste Section, and Joint Cheek.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do we calibrate the marking gauge directly against the mating board instead of measuring with a rule?
expected: Board thicknesses can vary by fractions of a millimetre; direct transfer ensures the baseline matches the exact physical dimension of the adjoining piece.
question: What is the physical benefit of scribing with a sharp spur instead of drawing a pencil line?
expected: The spur severs the surface wood fibres, which prevents surface tear-out and creates a physical groove for the saw blade to register into.
activities.scaffolding:
Step-by-step marking protocol:
1. Face Mark Datum: Confirm face side and face edge marks on all four boards.
2. Gauge Calibration: Set gauge pin to mating board thickness; lock thumb screw firmly.
3. Fence Contact: Keep the wooden fence tight against the datum face throughout the entire stroke.
4. Waste Shading: Clearly cross-hatch all waste sockets with pencil.
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate the marking gauge setup under the workshop document camera, projecting a high-magnification view of spur contact on the bench screen.
activities.transition: With baselines understood and annotated, we will now set up workpieces in bench vices and establish guided starter cuts.

activities.title: Guided Starter Kerfs and Vice Setup
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate clamping the timber board in the vice at a 45-degree angle to establish the first cut along the top corner. Model the thumb-guide technique: thumb knuckle resting against the saw blade plate well above the teeth, initiating the cut with 2-3 light pulling strokes strictly on the waste side of the pencil line. Circulate to inspect each student's first kerf, ensuring no student saws down the centre of the line.
activities.studentsDo: Clamp timber in the vice, position the tenon saw on the waste side of their marked socket line, and saw a starter kerf of no more than 2 mm depth. Complete the quality checklist before seeking teacher sign-off.
activities.visibleInstructions: Tick off each verification item on your Sawing Quality Control Checklist before cutting deeper than 2 mm into the timber.
activities.questioning:
q: Why must the saw blade sit entirely within the waste side rather than splitting the line?
expected: The kerf of the tenon saw blade is roughly 0.8 mm wide; sawing on the line removes wood from the pin, making the joint loose.
q: What physical feedback tells you the saw has initiated cleanly?
expected: The blade pulls smoothly in the created groove without jumping across the timber face.
activities.scaffolding:
Kerf Initiation Rules:
- Knuckle placement: Rest thumb knuckle high on the saw plate, never below the teeth line.
- Stroke direction: Pull backward gently to create the channel; do not push down aggressively.
- Kerf location: Leave the pencil layout line intact on the pin cheek.

activities.transition: Now that starter kerfs are verified on the waste side, proceed to independent sawing down to the baseline.

activities.teacherDoes: Supervise independent sawing across all four corner components. Provide individual corrective coaching on saw plate verticality and monitoring the scribed baseline. Intervene if students saw past the baseline. Model how to gently adjust the saw handle angle to correct a cut that starts to drift.

activities.visibleInstructions: Saw all vertical joint cheeks down to the scribed baseline on your project timber. Stop immediately when the blade reaches the scribed line on both faces. Open your workbooks and complete the 3-2-1 evaluation.
activities.questioning: How do you ensure you do not saw past the baseline on the hidden back face of the timber? Expected: Level the timber in the vice and periodically glance over the top of the board to track the cut progression on both faces simultaneously. If you notice your saw blade drifting toward the line, what corrective action should you take? Expected: Ease forward pressure, return to the upper section of the kerf, and lightly twist the handle to steer the teeth back into the waste.
activities.scaffolding:
Sawing Standards:
- Stopping point: Exactly at the scribed spur line—never 1 mm past.
- Blade orientation: Keep the saw plate square to the face of the board.
- Waste retention: Do not force or snap the waste wood; leave it intact for chisel removal.

lessons.title: Practical: Waste Removal, Corner Paring, and Dry Fitting
lessons.learningGoal: Use chisels and mallets to remove joint waste and pare cheeks for an accurate, flush dry-fit.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a closed ranking task in their workbooks, ordering four chisel waste removal steps from first rough chop to final vertical paring.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can safely chisel out waste wood and dry-fit my finger joints to achieve a flush alignment

activities.title: Chisel Safety and Waste Removal Mechanics
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate securing timber flat against a sacrificial backing board using a G-clamp. Model the stepped waste removal sequence: 1. Position chisel bevel-down 1-2 mm away from the baseline. 2. Tap lightly with a wooden mallet. 3. Turn board over and repeat from the opposite face. 4. Pare away the remaining waste core horizontally. Emphasise chisel safety: both hands must remain behind the cutting edge at all times. Script: 'Never place the chisel blade right in the scribed baseline on your first strike. The bevel acts as a wedge that forces the blade backwards across your line. We leave 1 mm of meat, then pare it vertically with hand pressure alone.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration, noting the bevel orientation and two-handed grip. Complete the workflow map in their workbooks outlining the waste removal sequence and decision branch for fitting.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the chisel waste removal workflow diagram in your workbook, identifying the correct tool orientation and the decision path when a joint binds.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must you chisel halfway through from one face before flipping the board to finish from the opposite side?
expected: Chiselling straight through from one side blows out and splinters the grain on the underside face.
question: Why must the bevel face away from the shoulder line during the final vertical paring pass?
expected: The flat back of the chisel must align against the flat vertical shoulder to produce a true 90-degree square floor.
activities.scaffolding:
Chisel Safety & Technique Rules:
- Hands behind edge: Non-dominant hand guides blade on bench; dominant hand controls mallet/handle.
- Sacrificial backing: Always clamp over a scrap board to protect the workbench and timber underside.
- Stepped paring: Step 1 = rough chop (bevel towards waste); Step 2 = horizontal chip removal; Step 3 = vertical finishing cut on baseline (flat back to shoulder).
activities.eLearning: Project diagram showing wedge-action forces of chisel bevels when struck with a mallet.
activities.transition: Now that the mechanical sequence is mapped in your workbooks, secure your components to the bench and prepare to trial your first dry-fit.

workbookSpec.title: Chisel Waste Removal Workflow
workbookSpec.prompt: Map the sequential workflow for chisel waste removal and fitting verification.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Clamp timber flat over sacrificial board with G-clamp. 2. Chop 1-2mm forward of baseline with mallet (flip board to chop from both sides). 3. Pare horizontal waste chips with bevel facing upward. 4. Vertical final pare on scribed baseline using flat back of chisel. Branch: If joint binds, inspect for burnished spots and pare high spots micro-thin; if joint closes flush, proceed to dry assembly check.

activities.title: Guided Trial Assembly and Diagnostics
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate the workshop as students begin dry-fitting their first corner. Intervene immediately if a student reaches for a mallet to force components together. Model how to hold the joint against natural light to detect gaps, and how to spot shiny 'burnished' wood fibres where cheeks are rubbing. Demonstrate paring micro-shavings (the thickness of paper) from the binding cheek to relieve pressure. Model recording diagnostic findings in the workbook table.
activities.studentsDo: Gently dry-fit corner joints using firm hand pressure only. Complete the diagnostic table in their workbooks by logging observed symptoms, identifying root causes, and executing specific paring remedies.
activities.visibleInstructions: Test-fit your first corner joint using hand pressure only. Complete the Diagnostic and Corrective Action Log in your workbook for any fit issues before paring.
activities.questioning: What does a shiny, compressed patch on the cheek of a timber pin tell you during dry-fitting? Expected: It is a high spot where the joint is binding; that exact spot needs light paring to let the components seat. Why will hammering a tight joint together with a mallet ruin your port frame? Expected: It will split the timber along the grain or permanently crush the wood fibres, preventing a square, flush alignment.
activities.scaffolding:
Diagnostic Guide:
- Joint won't enter: Cheeks too thick or socket too narrow -> Pare high spots off socket cheek.
- Joint won't seat to full depth: Socket floor has high waste wood in corners -> Clean out baseline corners with chisel corner.
- Joint enters skewed: One side of shoulder is cut deeper than the other -> Check shoulder line with try square and pare high side level.
activities.eLearning: Rear-of-room monitoring: circulate actively with spare combination squares to verify student diagnostic judgements.
activities.transition: With diagnostics logged, complete the iterative fitting of all four corners to achieve full frame alignment.

workbookSpec.title: Joint Diagnostic and Corrective Action Log

activities.title: Independent Iterative Fitting and Reflection
activities.teacherDoes: Provide one-on-one coaching to students as they refine all four corners. Check dry-assembled boxes for squareness across internal diagonals using a steel rule or combination square. Model checking squareness: 'Notice how measuring corner-to-corner diagonally tells us immediately if our shoulders are square.' Direct students to complete the 3-2-1 practical reflection in their workbooks as each corner reaches a flush friction-fit.
activities.studentsDo: Systematically pare, test, and refine all four corner finger joints until the four-sided frame dry-assembles flush under firm hand pressure. Complete the written reflection sections in their workbooks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Pare and test all four corners until your box frame dry-fits flush and square. Complete the 3-2-1 Practical Reflection in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
question: How do diagonal corner-to-corner measurements confirm your dry-assembled box is perfectly rectangular?
expected: If the two diagonal measurements taken from opposite inside corners are identical, the box is square (90 degrees at all corners).
question: If one diagonal measurement is 3 mm longer than the other, what does that indicate about the joint shoulders?
expected: The frame is racked into a parallelogram, meaning the shoulder cuts on one side are holding the joint out of square.
activities.scaffolding:
Iterative Fitting Protocol:
1. Test fit with hand pressure.
2. Disassemble and look for burnished contact spots.
3. Take one whisper shaving with a razor-sharp chisel.
4. Re-test. Repeat until components slide home flush.

activities.title: Diagnosing Joint Fit Issues
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the demonstration workbench. Present a dry-assembled box corner showing four distinct joint errors. Point to callout 1 (shoulder gap caused by shallow socket sawing), callout 2 (proud/flush offset from unequal stock thickness), callout 3 (split wood from forcing an over-tight interference fit), and callout 4 (angled joint resulting in an out-of-square corner). Model how to mark high spots with light pencil hatching and demonstrate paring a micro-shaving using a sharp 12mm bevel-edged chisel held flat against the joint cheek.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration of joint defects and paring techniques. Annotate the four callouts on the joint defect diagram in your workbook, writing the fault name and corrective action for each.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Look at the joint defect figure in your workbook matching the demonstration.
2. For each numbered callout (1 to 4), identify the specific joint assembly defect.
3. Write the defect name and the corrective workshop action on the provided lines.
activities.questioning: Why must you never force a tight finger joint together with a steel hammer or mallet during dry-fitting? Expected: Forcing the joint induces cross-grain tension that can split the pins along the grain lines and deform the shoulder lines. What causes a gap to appear along the joint shoulder even when the pins look fully seated? Expected: A socket cut that was stopped short of the baseline or waste timber left in the root of the socket preventing complete seating.
activities.scaffolding:
Diagnostic Reference:
- Callout 1: Shoulder Gap -> Check socket root for unpared waste; pare baseline flat.
- Callout 2: Proud/Misaligned End Grain -> Stock thickness variance; light sanding/planing required after glue-up.
- Callout 3: Split Pin/Cheek -> Excessive interference fit; pare cheek high spots with a chisel.
- Callout 4: Out-of-Square Assembly -> Socket walls cut out of square; pare cheeks to 90 degrees.

workbookSpec.title: Finger Joint Tolerance Analysis

3. Split Timber: Interference fit too tight; forced assembly. Correction: Pare high spots on joint cheeks before pressing.
4. Out-of-Square Skew: Joint cheeks cut at an angle. Correction: Pare cheeks perpendicular using a try square as a guide.

lessons.title: Practical: Gluing, Clamping, and Squaring the Frame
lessons.learningGoal: Construct a square timber port frame using wood adhesive, sash clamps, and diagonal measurement techniques.

orientate.smartStart: On the whiteboard diagram of a clamped rectangular frame, Diagonal 1 (top-left to bottom-right) measures 425mm and Diagonal 2 (top-right to bottom-left) measures 418mm. In your workbook, identify: 1. Which diagonal is long? 2. Across which diagonal corners must sash clamp pressure be increased to pull the frame into square?

activities.title: Clamping Sequence and Assembly Flow
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central glue-up station. Demonstrate applying a thin, even spread of PVA adhesive to the mating faces of finger joints using a small brush, explaining: 'Glue both contacting cheeks, but do not flood the joint; hydraulic pressure can prevent full seating.' Model fitting the frame together, placing sacrificial pine pads between sash clamp jaws and the project timber, and applying initial tension. Model measuring diagonals from inside corner to inside corner with a steel rule. Trace the assembly logic on the whiteboard flow chart, demonstrating the decision branch if diagonals are unequal.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher modeling adhesive spreading, sash clamp placement, and diagonal measurement. Complete the assembly workflow chart in the workbook by filling in the missing operational stages and decision paths.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Watch the live demonstration of adhesive application, clamp block placement, and diagonal checking.
2. Complete the Frame Assembly Workflow chart in your workbook.
3. Fill in the missing steps and label the decision path for correcting an out-of-square frame.
activities.questioning: Why must sacrificial timber blocks always be placed between the steel clamp jaws and the port sides? Expected: Steel clamp jaws exert high concentrated pressure that will crush and bruise the finished timber surface of the project. What happens if you apply excessive clamping pressure to the finger joints? Expected: It squeezes out virtually all adhesive from the joint cheeks, resulting in a 'starved' glue joint with severely reduced mechanical strength.
activities.scaffolding:
Assembly Workflow Stages:
1. Dry test layout -> 2. Apply even PVA coat to all joint mating surfaces -> 3. Seat joints by hand and fit sash clamps with pine pads -> 4. Measure diagonals A and B -> Decision: Are diagonals equal within 1mm? -> If NO: Angle clamp or tighten along the long diagonal -> If YES: Wipe squeeze-out with damp rag and transfer to drying rack.
activities.eLearning: Demonstration only. Workshop environment protocol: safety glasses worn, sleeves rolled up, hair tied back.

activities.title: Checking for Squareness
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through taking their initial clamp setup and taking baseline diagonal measurements. Demonstrate how to position the hook of the steel rule precisely into the inside corner vertex. Walk between benches to verify diagonal readings: 'Student A has D1 = 415mm, D2 = 419mm. We need to shift clamp pressure onto the 419mm axis.' Model recording these values into the audit table and performing the term-matching check to confirm understanding of clamping physics.
activities.studentsDo: Set sash clamps onto the frame with protective pads. Measure Diagonal 1 (corner A-C) and Diagonal 2 (corner B-D) using a steel rule. Record the measurements into the workbook table, calculate the difference, and complete the technical term matching.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Position your sash clamps over the joints using protective pine pads under every jaw.
2. Apply moderate tension to seat the joints.
3. Measure Diagonal 1 (Corner A to C) and record the millimetre value in your table.
4. Measure Diagonal 2 (Corner B to D) and record the millimetre value in your table.
5. Calculate the difference: if difference > 1mm, adjust clamp tension on the long diagonal.
6. Match the four workshop terms to their definitions in the table.
activities.questioning:
q: If Diagonal 1 is 420mm and Diagonal 2 is 415mm, why does tightening the clamp on Diagonal 1 pull the assembly back into square?
expected: The clamp compresses the longer axis, pulling those two corners closer together and pushing the acute corners outward until all angles reach 90 degrees.
q: Why is checking with a try square on the corners less reliable across a large frame than checking diagonals?
expected: A small 150mm try square only checks the local 90-degree corner, whereas diagonal measurement magnifies small angular errors across the entire length of the frame.
activities.scaffolding:
Squaring Formula:
- Diagonal 1 (D1) = Corner A to C
- Diagonal 2 (D2) = Corner B to D
- True Square: |D1 - D2| <= 1.0mm
Clamp Correction Rule: Always apply clamping force parallel to or across the LONGER diagonal to shorten it.

activities.questioning:
question: Why must you wipe glue squeeze-out with a damp rag while it is wet rather than scraping it off after it cures?
expected: Cured PVA is rock-hard and will tear out wood fibres when chiselled; also, dried glue seals the grain and prevents timber stains or clear finishes from penetrating evenly.
question: What will happen to the top and base panels next week if your frame cures out of square by 5mm?
expected: The pre-squared plywood top and base panels will not align with the frame edges, leaving overhangs or gaps that require extensive planing and compromise the design.

3. Diagonal verification: D1 = D2 (+/- 1mm).
4. Squeeze-out check: Clean internal corners thoroughly—any glue lump will block internal dividers.
5. Flat curing: Lay the clamped assembly completely flat on the rack so the frame does not twist.

What is the key distinction between a hazard and a risk? Expected: A hazard is a source of potential harm, whereas risk is the measurement of the likelihood and severity of that harm occurring.
Why is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) considered the final control measure in the hierarchy? Expected: PPE does not eliminate or isolate the hazard; it only provides a barrier, making it the least reliable and last line of defence.

Why is the residual risk rating usually lower than the initial risk rating? Expected: Because the implementation of control measures reduces either the likelihood or the consequence of the hazard.

activities.title: Modelled Measurement & Mark-out
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the assembly bench. Model the measurement process using a steel rule: 'When measuring the internal rebate, always measure at the top and bottom of the frame to account for potential racking or lack of squareness.' Demonstrate marking the plywood: 'We mark the width and length, then add a 1mm tolerance line outside the primary mark. This gives us room to hand-plane the edge for a flush, gap-free fit.' Project the diagram onto the screen.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher's positioning of the steel rule. Locate the internal rebate diagram in the workbook. Use the callout tool to identify the measurement points and tolerances on the diagram.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the diagram of the port frame rebate. Use the callout boxes to identify the four critical points of measurement and the location for the 1mm tolerance line. Label each point clearly.
activities.questioning:
Why is it critical to measure both the top and bottom width of the rebate? Expected: Frames are rarely perfectly square; the top and bottom may differ by a millimetre or two. Cutting to one measurement could result in a loose fit or binding.
What is the purpose of adding a 1mm tolerance to your marking lines? Expected: It provides extra material for final refinement with a plane or sanding block to ensure a precise, flush fit against the rebate shoulder.
activities.scaffolding:
Measurement Procedure:
1. Check for Square: Measure diagonally corner-to-corner to verify the frame is square.
2. Measure Internal Rebate: Take width measurements at top and bottom positions.
3. Measure Length: Take length measurements at left and right positions.
4. Account for Tolerance: Add 1mm outside the measured line for final hand-fitting.
5. Project Lines: Use a try-square to transfer marks across the timber grain.

lessons.title: Sanding Mechanics and Surface Preparation
lessons.learningGoal: Apply progressive grit sanding techniques to achieve a flush, stain-free exterior timber finish.

orientate.smartStart: A classmate has a deep scratch and some dried glue on their timber frame. If they start sanding with 240 grit sandpaper, explain what will happen.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can use progressive sandpaper grits (80, 120, and 240) in the correct order to remove glue stains and prepare my port for a professional finish

activities.title: Sanding Mechanics & Grit Progression
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the effect of sanding with the grain versus across the grain using a scrap timber sample. Project a microscopic view of timber grain to illustrate cell structure. Model the transition: start with an 80-grit abrasive to remove mill marks and glue, then proceed to 120-grit to remove 80-grit scratches, and finish with 240-grit for final polish. Emphasise that jumping grits (e.g., 80 to 240) leaves underlying damage that stain will highlight. Demonstrate wrapping paper tightly around a sanding block to ensure flat faces and crisp edges.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the demonstration, then complete the guided notes in their workbooks regarding the relationship between grit size, abrasive sequence, and grain integrity.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the terms provided in the word bank, complete the sentences in your workbook to define the technical process of timber surface preparation.
activities.questioning:
Why must we always sand parallel to the wood grain? Expected: Sanding across the grain severs wood fibres at an angle, creating deep scratches that remain visible, particularly after oil or stain application.
What is the consequence of 'skipping' a grit level (e.g., moving from 80 to 240 directly)? Expected: The finer grit will fail to remove the deep furrows created by the coarse grit, leaving unsightly scratches under a finish.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Grit: The size of abrasive particles on sandpaper; lower numbers are coarser, higher numbers are finer.
2. Grain: The longitudinal direction of wood fibres.
3. Progression: The sequential use of increasingly finer abrasives to refine the surface.
activities.transition: Now that we understand the necessity of sequential sanding, we will move to the workshop benches to practice this progression on our actual port components.

The concept of grit {{4}} is critical; you must work through intermediate stages using {{5}} grits (120 then 240) to effectively eliminate marks left by the previous abrasive.

activities.title: Ordering Sanding Operations
activities.teacherDoes: Display a mock-up frame showing typical surface defects: dried glue squeeze-out and visible pencil layout lines. Model the logic of progressive grit sanding by demonstrating that coarse abrasives are required to level physical irregularities first, while finer grits are reserved for refining surface texture. Script: 'If we jump to fine grit too early, we merely polish the glue and pencil lines into the timber surface. We must remove obstructions first.'
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the provided operational list and rank them into the logical sequence required to transform a rough timber assembly into a smooth, ready-to-finish surface, as presented in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rank the surface preparation steps in the correct chronological order by numbering the slots 1 to 5.
activities.questioning:
What is the consequence of sanding over hardened PVA glue squeeze-out with a fine grit abrasive? Expected: The glue will clog (or gum up) the abrasive particles, rendering the sandpaper ineffective and creating uneven burnished marks on the timber.
Why is it mandatory to sand parallel to the grain during the final stages of surface preparation? Expected: Sanding across the grain leaves deep, visible scratches that are highlighted when stains or oils are applied, whereas parallel sanding ensures scratches blend into the natural grain.
activities.scaffolding:
Sequence Steps Overview:
1. Rough Material Removal (Scrapers/Chisels): Address glue squeeze-out and height differences.
2. Flattening/Levelling (Coarse Grit - 80): Even out joint surfaces.
3. Refining/Smoothing (Medium Grit - 120): Remove previous scratch patterns.
4. Polishing (Fine Grit - 240): Prepare timber pores for final coating.
5. Cleaning (Final Step): Remove dust to prevent finish contamination.

activities.questioning:
What defects become visible under a raking light that are otherwise invisible under standard overhead workshop lighting?
Expected: Raking light casts long shadows across subtle surface irregularities such as sanding scratches, dried glue film, or shallow depressions.

Why must you remove 80-grit scratches completely before progressing to 120-grit?
Expected: Higher grit papers cannot remove deep scratches from lower grits; they only polish the edges of the scratches, leaving visible defects under oil or clear coat.
activities.scaffolding:
Raking Light Audit Guide:
1. Position your port at a low angle to a strong light source.
2. Observe the shadows cast; dark lines indicate scratches or voids.
3. If swirl marks appear, switch to manual block-sanding in the direction of the grain.
4. Surface Readiness: The wood should feel silky and uniform to the touch, with no visible glue patches or pencil marks.

activities.title: CAD Terminology & Axis Precision
activities.teacherDoes: Project SketchUp for Web on the board. Demonstrate initiating a project and identify the Red (length), Green (width), and Blue (height) axes. Model turning a 2D 300x200mm rectangle into a 3D solid using the Push/Pull tool. Contrast loose geometry with a 'Group'. Script: 'In design engineering, digital precision dictates physical reality. If your CAD dimensions lack tolerance, your physical port parts will bind or fail. We match terms to ensure our digital model accurately guides production.' Rear-of-room visual check as students match definitions.
activities.studentsDo: Read each CAD term in column 1 of the workbook table and write the matching letter (A–E) in the Match column using the definition bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each CAD term in the left column to its correct engineering definition from the bank by writing the corresponding letter (A–E) in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why will components fail to assemble physically if CAD tolerance is set to zero? Expected: Zero tolerance leaves no clearance for glue lines, material expansion, or cutting kerf, causing parts to bind or crack.
How does axis locking (Red, Green, Blue) maintain geometric squareness? Expected: It forces lines and extrusions to remain strictly perpendicular and parallel rather than drifting off-angle.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions to record:
- Extrusion: Converting a 2D profile into a 3D solid volume along a specified vector.
- Orthographic Projection: Multi-view 2D drawings (top, front, side) depicting a 3D object to scale.
- Tolerance: Allowable variation in manufactured dimensions ensuring interlocking fit.
- Axis Alignment: Constraining drawing geometry along Red (X), Green (Y), and Blue (Z) planes.
- Component Grouping: Isolating geometry so individual parts do not merge or distort adjacent surfaces.

lessons.title: Hardware Mechanisms: Hinge and Clasp Assembly

orientate.smartStart: Concept attainment task in workbook: Examine the three technical diagrams of fitted butt hinges displayed on the board (A: recessed too deep, B: recessed half knuckle, C: surface mounted without rebate). Identify which hinge will bind and explain the mechanical reason.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can calculate hinge recess depths and evaluate clasp tension to prevent binding and ensure flush lid closure

activities.title: Hinge Mechanics: Binding, Rebating, & Clearance
activities.teacherDoes: Present physical demonstration blocks with mounted butt hinges. Demonstrate 'binding' by attempting to close a lid where the hinge knuckle sits below the timber rebate plane. Script: 'If the knuckle axis is buried beneath the timber edge, the wood edges collide before the leaf completes 180 degrees of travel. This is binding. To achieve a flush closure, the recess must be calculated precisely.' Walk the room verifying student workbook entries.
activities.studentsDo: Listen to the physical demonstration, inspect the hinge leaf and pin mechanism, and match the mechanical terminology to their definitions in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each hardware mechanism term in the left column to its definition in the bank by writing the corresponding letter (A-D) in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
prompt: What mechanical force causes a timber lid to crack if forced shut while the hinge is binding?
expected: Lever mechanical advantage concentrates immense stress along the rear joint baseline, shearing the screw threads or splitting the timber along the grain.
prompt: Why must the hinge pin (knuckle axis) sit directly aligned with the rear seam of the box?
expected: If the pivot point is offset, the arc of rotation shifts, pulling the lid away from flush alignment.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for reference:
- Binding: Mechanical interference where timber faces collide before the hinge closes fully, preventing complete travel.
- Knuckle: The cylindrical hollow loop through which the hinge pin passes to form the pivot point.
- Rebate: A recessed step cut into the timber edge allowing the hinge leaf to sit flush with the surface.
- Operational Clearance: The engineered gap (typically 0.5mm-1mm) that prevents friction between moving timber surfaces.
activities.eLearning: Display high-resolution technical diagrams of hinge knuckle positions on the projector.
activities.transition: Pre-warn: In 1 minute, transition from definitions to calculating exact rebate formulas in your workbook.

activities.title: Hinge Rebate Depth & Calculation
activities.teacherDoes: Project a dimensioned cross-section of a 50mm butt hinge with a 4mm knuckle diameter and 1.2mm leaf thickness. Model the standard rule: 'Leaf rebate depth equals the thickness of one leaf (1.2mm). The knuckle centreline must sit proud of the box exterior.' Model the failure modes: too shallow leaves an unsightly gap; too deep causes binding. Guide students through completing the guided cloze notes and verifying caliper readings.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the modelled engineering drawing, fill in the blanks in the cloze notes, and calculate the required rebate depth for the supplied workshop butt hinges.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing technical words in your workbook guided notes using the word bank to articulate the calculation of hinge rebates.
activities.questioning:
If our hinge leaf thickness is 1.5mm, what exact depth must the chisel rebate be pared to? Expected: Exactly 1.5mm so that the metal leaf sits flush with the timber face.
What happens to the port lid seal if one hinge is rebated to 1.5mm but the second hinge is rebated to 2.5mm? Expected: The lid will sit twisted/canted, creating a gap on one side and binding on the other.
activities.scaffolding:
Formulae & reference:
- Rebate Depth = Leaf Thickness (typically 1.2mm to 1.5mm)
- Knuckle Clearance = Knuckle axis must align outside the timber seam
- Defect 1: Rebate too shallow → Visible gap between lid and base frame
- Defect 2: Rebate too deep → Timber edges collide causing hinge binding

activities.title: Clasp Alignment & Tension Mechanics
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate a toggle clasp (briefcase catch). Show how the hook must pull the loop over-centre under slight spring tension to prevent vibration loosening. Model three configurations on sample boards: Configuration A (dead centre, 1mm tension pull), Configuration B (skewed 5 degrees off-centre), Configuration C (latch mounted too far down, no catch engagement). Facilitate the analytical ranking activity in student workbooks.
activities.studentsDo: Examine the three clasp mounting configurations in the workbook, rank them from best mechanical function (1) to worst (3), and write an engineering justification explaining why the worst configuration will fail.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rank the three clasp configurations from most functional (Rank 1) to least functional (Rank 3). Underneath, write a two-sentence justification explaining the mechanical failure mode of the configuration you placed at Rank 3.
activities.questioning:
Why must a toggle clasp close with a positive 'snap' of tension rather than resting loose? Expected: Tension keeps the catch locked over-centre so carrying vibrations do not cause the port to spill its contents.
What occurs if the catch plate is installed off-centre relative to the lid hook? Expected: Lateral stress is applied to the clasp rivets, twisting the latch mechanism and causing premature failure.
activities.scaffolding:
Evaluation criteria for clasps:
1. Axial Alignment: Upper hook and lower latch share the exact same vertical centreline.
2. Over-Centre Tension: Hook engages the lip and requires positive manual pressure to snap shut.
3. Clearance: Lever clears the bottom timber edge during swing-away release.

lessons.title: Workshop Practice: Hardware Installation & Pilot-Drilling
lessons.learningGoal: Apply precision marking out, pilot-drilling, and fastening processes to install butt hinges and clasps flush onto a timber port.

activities.title: Modelled Hinge Layout & Marking-Out
activities.teacherDoes: Gather students around the central workbench. Model marking hinge locations on the rear of the port frame. Measure 40mm in from each outer corner using a steel rule. Position the hinge leaf flush with the top edge. Scribe the perimeter using a marking knife held tight against the brass leaf. Script: 'A pencil line is 0.5mm wide and crushes fibres; a marking knife severs fibres precisely to guide the chisel paring. Notice I check squareness with a try square before committing.' Model scribing the rebate baseline with a marking gauge set to the leaf thickness.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration, noting marking knife posture, rule placement, and gauge setting. In their workbooks, sequence the procedural steps for marking out a hinge recess.
activities.visibleInstructions: Sequence the procedural steps for marking out a hinge rebate in your workbook by ordering the steps from 1 to 4.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do we score the layout lines with a marking knife instead of a 2B pencil?
Expected: The knife severs timber grain cleanly, preventing surface tearout when paring the waste with a chisel.
q: Why are hinges positioned at least 40mm in from the corner joint?
Expected: Placing hardware too close to the finger joints risks splitting the end-grain pins and weakens the structural corner.
activities.scaffolding:
Marking sequence:
1. Measure: Steel rule set to 40mm from outer frame edge
2. Align: Hinge leaf aligned with knuckle pin proud of rear face
3. Scribe: Marking knife cuts side shoulder lines
4. Gauge: Marking gauge scribes depth line matching leaf thickness
activities.eLearning: Demonstration conducted at central bench. Workshop safety glasses required before entering demonstration perimeter.
activities.transition: Pre-warn: In 1 minute, collect your safety glasses, steel rule, and marking knife, and move to your allocated bench station.

activities.title: Guided Pilot-Drilling & Depth Stop Calibration
activities.teacherDoes: Model measuring the screw core with digital calipers. Script: 'To select the correct twist bit, measure the root shaft diameter between threads, not the outer thread. If the screw root is 2.0mm, choose a 2.0mm bit.' Demonstrate setting the drill press mechanical depth stop: Screw Length (15mm) minus Hinge Leaf (1.2mm) = 13.8mm depth. Lock the knurled stop nut. Model centre-punching the marked screw centres. Oversee student pairs as they verify drill bit selection and depth stops.
activities.studentsDo: Work in pairs at designated drill press stations. Measure screw root diameter with digital calipers, calculate required drill depth, set the depth stop, and tick off each safety and accuracy criterion in the workbook checklist before drilling.
activities.visibleInstructions: With your partner, verify your hardware measurements and machine setup. Tick each item on the Hardware Pre-Drilling Checklist in your workbook before pressing the start button on the drill press.
activities.questioning:
What occurs if the pilot drill diameter is equal to the outer thread diameter? Expected: The screw threads will have no wood to bite into, stripping the hole and failing to hold.
What occurs if you drill deeper than the calculated depth stop? Expected: The bit will penetrate through the exterior face of the timber port, ruining the finish and weakening the fastener anchor.
activities.scaffolding:
Setup equations & checks:
- Screw Root = Central core diameter without threads (e.g. 2.0mm)
- Pilot Bit Size = Exactly equal to screw root
- Depth Stop = Screw length minus hinge leaf thickness
- Centre Punch = Indentation prevents drill bit from 'wandering' off centre
activities.eLearning: Demonstrate the drill press depth stop adjustment live under workshop safety conditions.
activities.transition: Pre-warn: Once your checklist is completely signed off by your partner, drill pilot holes and proceed to bench screw installation.

workbookSpec.title: Hardware Pilot-Drilling Pre-Flight Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete and tick every safety and calibration check with your workbench partner prior to operating the drill press.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All 6 items verified, calculated, and ticked by partner prior to operating machinery.
items: Screw root diameter measured with digital calipers (excluding thread flights).
Twist drill bit diameter matched exactly to the measured screw root dimension.
Drill press depth stop calculated: (Screw length - leaf thickness) and locked.
Workpiece marked with an automatic centre-punch at exact fastener centres.

Safety glasses donned, long hair tied back, and loose clothing secured.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: All 6 checklist items must be ticked and verified by peer/teacher observation before drilling commences. Depth stop must be visually inspected to confirm drill bit cannot exit through the timber face.

activities.title: Independent Fastening, Fitting, & Alignment Review
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate actively across workbenches. Enforce the use of hand screwdrivers rather than cordless impact drivers to protect small brass screw heads. Demonstrate the 'loosen-align-retighten' micro-adjustment technique for hinges: slightly back off middle screws, close lid to check flush seams, clamp flush, then tighten home. Assist students in evaluating their completed hinge and clasp assembly against tolerances.
activities.studentsDo: Hand-drive screws into pre-drilled pilot holes to secure both butt hinges and front clasp. Test lid opening and closure for binding, check seam flushness, and record an assembly evaluation in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Drive screws by hand using the correct size screwdriver. Test your lid operation. Record your 3 assembly observations, 2 mechanical adjustments made, and 1 root cause analysis in your workbook review section.
activities.questioning:
Why do we avoid using high-speed cordless drivers for small brass hardware screws? Expected: Brass is soft; power drivers easily strip the screw head drive slots or snap the head off under excessive torque.
If the lid overhangs the base by 1mm on the right side, which hinge must be adjusted and in which direction? Expected: Loosen the right hinge screws and shift the leaf 1mm rearward or adjust the opposing hinge forward until square.
activities.scaffolding:
Assembly quality checks:
- Screw heads seated flush in leaf countersinks (no raised sharp edges)
- Lid closes flat along all four edges without spring-back (no binding)
- Clasp snaps shut with positive engagement over the hook
- Screwdrivers: Size #1 Pozidriv or Phillips to match screw head exactly

activities.title: Technical Vocabulary of Internal Organisation
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the four key technical terms for internal storage engineering: Modular Design, Utility, Clearance, and Half-Lap Joint. Display physical examples of a fixed solid timber partition versus a removable 3mm plywood divider. Model the distinction between nominal dimension and working clearance.

activities.visibleInstructions: Match each term in the 'Term' column to its definition from the bank below. Write the matching definition letter in the 'Match' column.
activities.questioning:
Why is 3mm structural plywood selected over solid timber stock for internal dividers? Expected: Plywood has cross-laminated grain that prevents dimensional movement, cupping, and splitting across thin sections.
What is the functional difference between static and modular dividers in custom case design? Expected: Static dividers are permanently bonded, whereas modular dividers use friction or slots to allow user reconfiguration as storage needs change.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Modular Design: A system designed with interchangeable sub-units that can be arranged or reconfigured independently.
- Utility: The functional efficiency and practical usefulness of a storage container for a specific end user.
- Clearance: The deliberate dimensional tolerance or gap left between mating parts to allow insertion without binding.
- Half-Lap Joint: A joinery technique where half the thickness of each interlocking piece is removed to create a flush junction.

activities.title: I Do: Machine Anatomy and Operational Safety Zones
activities.teacherDoes:
Gather students around the central demonstration scroll saw and laser cutter. Demonstrate adjusting the scroll saw hold-down foot flush against 3mm plywood scrap to eliminate chatter. Identify the 50mm operator danger zone around the blade. Walk over to the laser cutter to identify the lid interlock switch, extraction damper, and emergency stop button. Explicitly model operator stance and line-of-sight.

Modelled Example:
Teacher: 'Notice how I adjust Callout 1, the hold-down foot, so it rests flat against the 3mm plywood. If this is loose, the blade will lift the stock on the upstroke, causing chatter and potential splitting. For Callout 4, the E-stop, my palm strikes it downwards in an emergency to instantly isolate power.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher demonstration. On the workbook machine schematics, record the four critical safety components and boundary limits indicated on the live demonstration equipment.
activities.visibleInstructions: Label the four indicated callouts on the machine safety schematic in your workbook with the correct component names and safety purposes.
activities.questioning:
Why must the scroll saw hold-down foot rest firmly on top of the thin plywood workpiece? Expected: It counteracts the upward stroke of the reciprocating blade, preventing work chatter, edge splintering, and operator loss of control.
What is the function of the magnetic interlock switch on the laser cutter enclosure? Expected: It breaks the electrical circuit to the laser tube instantly if the lid is lifted during a job, preventing hazardous beam exposure.
activities.scaffolding:
Key Machine Components:
1. Hold-Down Foot: Secures thin sheet stock firmly against the scroll saw bed.
2. Blade Guard & Tension Lever: Protects operator fingers and maintains blade rigidity.
3. Exhaust Damper / Extraction: Extracts smoke and particulate matter outside the workshop.
4. Emergency Stop (E-Stop): Isolates mains electrical supply instantaneously in an emergency.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 4-stage preparation sequence under raking workbench light: 1. Inspecting under 45-degree angled light to spot machine cross-grain scratches. 2. activities.questioning:
Why does raking light reveal flaws that overhead lighting conceals? Expected: Low-angle light casts shadows into depressions, machine chatter marks, and cross-grain scratches, making surface defects visible.
Why is an oil-soaked rag an immediate workshop combustion hazard if left crumpled? Expected: The solvent and oil cure through exothermic oxidation, generating heat that cannot dissipate when crumpled, causing spontaneous combustion.

Stage 2: Progressive sanding (180 -> 240 -> 320 -> 400 grit with grain).
Stage 3: Tack cloth decontamination (resin cloth lifts dust from pores).

activities.title: Fastener Mechanics Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly explain how screws anchor into wood fibres compared to nails. Demonstrate pilot hole sizing against screw core diameter and countersinking for flush hardware. Script: 'A nail wedges fibres apart, which can split thin timber. A wood screw cuts threads into the fibres. We must drill a pilot hole matching the screw's inner shank so threads bite without hydraulic splitting.'
activities.studentsDo: Review the structural fastener concepts and complete the matching table in the workbook by pairing each fastener term to its correct definition from the provided bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each fastener term in the table to its correct mechanical function from the definition bank by writing the matching letter in the Match column.
activities.questioning:
Why does driving a screw into hardwood without a pilot hole split the grain? Expected: Hardwood fibres cannot compress easily; the solid shank displaces timber volume, exerting outward tensile force that splits along the grain.
What is the mechanical purpose of a countersink when installing hinges? Expected: It creates a conical recess allowing a flat-head screw to sit flush with the hardware face so the port lid closes fully.
activities.scaffolding:
Pilot Hole: A relief hole drilled to the root diameter of the screw to prevent timber splitting.
Countersink: A conical bevel cut at the hole mouth allowing flat screw heads to sit flush.
Thread Engagement: Helical ridges biting into wood fibres to resist axial pull-out forces.

activities.title: Joinery Hierarchy and Grain Guided Notes
activities.teacherDoes: Present the structural hierarchy of timber joints: butt joint versus finger joint. Illustrate why end-grain provides poor fastener holding power and weak glue bonds compared to face-grain. Script: 'Wood fibres act like a bundle of drinking straws. Fasteners or glue going directly into end-grain pull out easily because there is no cross-fibre friction. Finger joints alternate grain contact and maximise long-grain glue surface.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow the whiteboard explanation and complete the cloze passage on joinery forces, grain orientation, and fastener pull-out resistance.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the word bank provided to complete the guided cloze notes on timber grain orientation and joinery performance.
activities.questioning:
Why do screws pull out of end-grain much more easily than edge-grain? Expected: In end-grain, threads slide parallel between the vertical tubular fibres without biting across the grain structure.
Why is the finger joint used on the port corners rather than a simple butt joint? Expected: Finger joints provide interlocking physical fingers and expose large edge-grain glue surface area, resisting racking loads.
activities.scaffolding:
Hierarchy summary:
- Butt joint: Low strength; weak end-grain glue adhesion; relies heavily on fasteners.
- Finger joint: High strength; mechanical interlocking fingers + high side-grain glue area.
- Fastener orientation: Side grain = maximum grip; End grain = minimal pull-out resistance.

activities.title: Hardware Integrity Inspection Modeling
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate mechanical inspection criteria on a sample timber port at the front workbench. Show how to check the rear hinge gap using a 1.5mm feeler/shim: 'Observe that if the shim binds at either end, the hinge pin axis is not parallel with the timber edge, which induces strain on the timber screws.' Demonstrate testing the briefcase clasp engagement: 'Listen for the distinct snap. If the latch requires forced downward pressure, the strike plate is misaligned by under 1mm.' Finally, inspect screw seatings with a try square and steel rule, highlighting perpendicular alignment and countersinking depth.

prompt: Why does an out-of-parallel hinge pin axis weaken the timber over time?

expected: It indicates insufficient downward compression, allowing internal contents to shift and the lid to rattle during transport.

activities.title: Defining Product Evaluation Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce technical evaluative terms on the board: Dimensional Tolerance, Structural Divergence, Timber Grain Distortion, and Aesthetic Deviation. Contrast vague evaluation statements with professional technical analysis: 'Do not write "the corner did not fit right"; write "the corner exhibited a 1.5mm structural divergence due to cumulative saw kerf loss exceeding dimensional tolerance."'

activities.questioning:
q: Why is separating aesthetic deviation from structural divergence essential when evaluating a timber product?
Expected: Aesthetic issues affect surface finish and appearance, while structural divergence affects strength, squareness, and load capacity.
q: What role does dimensional tolerance play in evaluating whether a manufactured product is acceptable?
Expected: It establishes the allowable variance (+/- 1.5mm) within which parts assemble and function correctly.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Dimensional Tolerance = allowable variance in dimensions (+/- 1.5mm); Structural Divergence = difference in physical joinery or geometry from CAD drawings; Timber Grain Distortion = warping, cupping, or movement along wood fibres; Aesthetic Deviation = surface finish variances, tool marks, or coating sheen differences.

activities.title: Prioritising Manufacturing Evaluation Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Define the five core manufacturing evaluation criteria: Structural Integrity (load capacity), Joinery Precision (assembly tightness/squareness), Surface Finish Quality (sanding and coating consistency), Mechanical Operation (smooth hardware travel), and Customisation Utility (user-focused internal layout). Demonstrate how a port designed for heavy fishing tackle prioritises Structural Integrity and Mechanical Operation, whereas an art display case prioritises Customisation Utility and Surface Finish.
activities.studentsDo: Analyse personal design brief intentions. Rank the five criteria from 1 (most critical) to 5 (least critical) based on their specific intended user storage requirements in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rank the five evaluation criteria from 1 (most critical) to 5 (least critical) according to your port's original design brief and user requirements.
activities.questioning: Why would Joinery Precision take precedence over Surface Finish for a timber port intended to carry heavy mechanical tools? Expected: Precision joinery provides maximum glue surface contact and mechanical interlocking, preventing joint failure under heavy loads. How does Customisation Utility reflect the success of the SBC Design Model? Expected: It proves the port was successfully adapted to solve the specific user problem identified in the initial brief.
activities.scaffolding: Criteria definitions: Structural Integrity = resistance to racking and loading forces; Joinery Precision = zero-gap fit and 90-degree alignment; Surface Finish = scratch-free 400-grit texture and uniform coating; Mechanical Operation = positive latch and unhindered hinge swing; Customisation Utility = effective compartment sizing for user items.
